3.14.2.en: * Glorious is the fruit of good labours, if this is counted worthy of struggling for it, and it is a part of true happiness.

3.15.0.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus But the children of adulterers do not attain their perfection, and the offspring of the unlawful bed shall become extinct. [16]

3.15.1.en: Here the wise man calls the foolish wicked adulterers, because they left wisdom, the beloved, beautiful bride, and cleaved to defiled lusts.

3.15.2.en: Origen sees that the adulterers here are those whose souls bend down to the lusts of the flesh and its pleasures, and leave their attachment to the Spirit, thus having turned away from their Bridegroom, God, with a spirit of adultery. Such souls hear the shameful saying: "thou hadst a whore's forehead, thou refusedst to be ashamed" (Jer 3:3).

3.15.3.en: * There is adultery of the body, and another adultery of the soul when it forms fellowship with Satan. For the soul is either partner and sister to Satan or to God and the angels. If it commits adultery with Satan it is not fit for the heavenly Bridegroom.

3.15.4.en: St. Macarius the Great Perhaps by the children of adulterers here he means their works, which will not endure, but perish, and the adulterers themselves perish with them.

3.16.0.en: 17 If they live long, they shall be counted as nothing, and in their last days their old age shall be without honor. 18 And if they die quickly, they shall have no hope and no comfort in the day of reckoning, 19 for the end of the wicked generation is dreadful.

3.16.1.en: And even if their life is long, they are counted as nothing, and at their end their old age is without honor. [17]

3.16.2.en: Since the righteous cleave to immortal righteousness, in heavenly wisdom they enjoy not length of life on earth, but heavenly immortality. As for the wicked adulterers, though their life be long on earth and they become elders and have abundant offspring, all this is counted as everything, and they become, in the day of the Lord, without honor.

3.17.0.en: And if they die quickly they shall have no hope, nor consolation in the day of judgment. [18]

3.17.1.en: Whether the time of the wicked's life be long or short, time inevitably passes, and they stand on the great day of the Lord in severe torment without consolation, for they have no hope.

3.18.0.en: For the end of the wicked generation is hard. [19]

3.18.1.en: The time of pleasures and temporal honors soon passes, and the wicked man and his children who imitated his evil stand in misery, asking the mountains to fall on them and the hills to cover them.

3.18.2.en: In Your hand I enjoy the spirit of strength, and I rise above pain

4.0.s.en: 1. The memory of the righteous and the memory of the wicked

4.0.0.en: 1 Virginity with virtue is more beautiful; for with it is an everlasting memorial, because it remains known with God and with men. 2 When it is present it is imitated, and when it is absent it is longed for, and throughout the ages it is proud of the crown of victory after its triumph in the arena of pure battles. 3 But the multitudinous brood of the hypocrites does not prosper, and their bastard slips do not take deep root, nor stand upon a firm stem, 4 and though they put forth branches for a time, because they are not firmly rooted the wind shakes them and the whirlwind plucks them up. 5 Their branches are broken off before their time, and their fruit is evil, not ripe to eat, and good for nothing. 6 And those born of the unlawful bed bear witness to the wickedness of their parents when their state is examined.

4.0.1.en: God created man to live immortal, untouched by death, but through the envy of the devil death entered into the world, and man chose with his full will to make a covenant with death, not with God the Giver of life. Now that man has felt his loss of immortality, strong feelings stir in his depths, and an overwhelming desire to immortalize his memory. Mankind has used every means to achieve this goal, such as the erection of magnificent triumphal arches, or carving on temples, or setting up precious statues, and above all this man came to look to his offspring as the best means of achieving the permanence of his memory. From here childlessness - in the minds of many - became a sign of a curse and of God's wrath upon man. Besides this, every Jew was awaiting that the Messiah, the Savior, would come from his offspring, and if he was deprived of offspring this hope was cut off from him.

4.0.2.en: Better is the deprivation of children, and the acquisition of virtue, for in its remembrance is immortality, because it is known with God and men. [1]

4.0.3.en: Here the wise man compares a wicked man who has many sons and grandsons in whom he takes pride, and thinks that they immortalize his memory, with a righteous man who has no offspring, but has set his heart on the holy life in the Lord as his true possessions and the subject of his immortality in heaven.

4.0.4.en: The offspring of the wicked are like fruits that do not endure, so that even if they live to old age they live a shameful life, or die at a young age without hope of immortality (Wis 3:16-19). So it is better for the righteous to care for spiritual fruits, that is, virtue, as his spiritual offspring, and his permanent deposit in heaven. For it is honorable and its reward is blessed immortality. This is what drove some to the life of virginity, to consecrate all their energies to the Lord.

4.0.5.en: * How can the soul that is immersed in the pleasures of the flesh and occupied only with human longings direct its gaze to the intellectual light, free from preoccupations...? The eyes of the pig, which always look downward, cannot see the wonders of heaven. So also the soul which the flesh pushes downward cannot lift its sight to see the heavenly beauty, but turns to the lowly, animal things.

4.0.6.en: The soul which wishes to devote its sight to the enjoyment of heavenly delights casts what is earthly behind its back, and does not share in what entangles it with worldly life. It turns all the powers of love in it from material things to intellectual contemplation of immaterial beauty. The virginity of the body helps to achieve the aims of such a soul.

4.0.7.en: Virginity aims to create a complete forgetfulness of natural passions in the soul, so it prevents the process of continual descent to satisfy bodily desires. And once the soul is freed from such things it does not hazard the undefiled heavenly delights by being ignorant of them and heedless of them, and it abstains from the habits that involve man in what the law of nature seems to some extent to concede... It is the purity of heart that prevails in life that alone then captivates the soul.

4.0.8.en: The Martyr St. Cyprian In the mind of St. Gregory of Nyssa virginity was bound up with the heavenly life, supporting man to practice the virginity of the soul, the heart, the mind, the senses and the desires, which believers enjoy by the Holy Spirit, the Giver of fellowship with the heavenly Father, who sanctifies our souls and our spirits and our bodies.

4.0.9.en: * Virginity is a necessary door to the life of holiness...

4.0.10.en: It is the channel that draws the divinity into fellowship with man.

4.0.11.en: It offers two wings that support man's desire to soar toward the heavenly things.

4.0.12.en: It is the bond of unity between what is divine and what is human, by it agreement is achieved after a great gulf had occurred between them.

4.0.13.en: * It has been demonstrated that the union of the soul with the incorruptible divinity cannot be achieved by any other way such as man's entering into this great purity. By this man comes to resemble God so as to receive the virginity that reflects the purity of God as in a mirror, so that his image is mingled with beauty through his meeting with the supreme Beauty and his contemplation of it.

4.0.14.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * Virginity is not honored for its own sake, but for its relation to God.

4.1.0.en: St. Augustine When it is present it is imitated, and when it is absent it is regretted, and in eternity it is received with the reception of the victor, crowned eternally, after its victory in a contest, no blemish mars its struggles. [2]

4.1.1.en: What a wonderful depiction of the man consecrated to the Lord, especially the virgin, who sold everything, even what is his right according to nature, to acquire union with God.

4.1.2.en: The man who is virtuous in the Lord is an object of men's admiration in this world even if they oppose him, and an object of wonder in heaven, where he enters eternity as a victorious king who triumphed in his battle against the devil and his angels by Christ Jesus who works in him.

4.1.3.en: By saying: "When it is present men imitate it," the wise man reveals that the object of men's admiration is not the righteous man himself, but the virtue that is present with him and precedes him, so that many desire to acquire it; they see it manifested in the righteous man, so they imitate him that they may enjoy it.

4.1.4.en: And by saying: "And when it is absent they long for it," the wise man points to the efficacy of virtue or holiness, for even if they no longer see the righteous man, in his absence from them they feel as though virtue itself had gone away from them, and so they long for it. And perhaps he means here that the wicked compare the presence of virtue in the righteous man with its absence from them, and so long for it and ask to acquire it.

4.1.5.en: Since virtue in its reality is "the person of the Lord Christ," as Origen says, on the great day of the Lord the heavenly ones will receive the holy Church, victorious over evil, and will see her Christ manifested in her, counting her victory as the victory of Christ. And they will regard her crown as though it were a crown for the Lord Christ!

4.1.6.en: In other words, our life on earth is a battlefield whose two sides are the Lord Christ and the devil; He allows us the spiritual battle, and it is He who grants us the power to strive, and it is He who is victorious in us, and it is He who presents to us the crown, and it is He who is crowned in us!

4.1.7.en: * To seek Christ is like seeking the Word and wisdom and justice and truth and the omnipotence of God. For Christ is all these.

4.1.8.en: * As the Savior is "righteousness" and truth and holiness in one, so He is also "stability" (Jer 17:3) LXX. So it is impossible to become righteous or holy without Christ. Just as it is impossible to "stand firm" without Him, for He is "the stability of Israel."

4.1.9.en: * You are righteousness, and we have followed You as righteousness, and also as holiness and wisdom and peace and truth and the way that leads to God, the true life.

4.2.0.en: Origen But the numerous offspring of the wicked do not flourish, and they are a bastard brood, so they do not send down deep roots, nor stand on a firm stem. [3]

4.2.1.en: After he portrayed for us the destiny of the righteous, and that their memory, though it lasts on earth, yet what is greater, remains immortal in heaven, they truly become eternally crowned kings, now he speaks to us of the destiny of the wicked.

4.2.2.en: The wicked often boast of begetting a multitude of legitimate children, as though they had achieved success in everything, even in begetting those who will immortalize their memory. But since the wicked did not accept God as their Father and the Church as their Mother, their children become bastards, that is, illegitimate children. They bequeath to them the perishable temporal things, and do not give them the roots of living faith, so they do not enjoy the new birth, which provides a firm stem and surpassing spiritual fruit. For this reason the children of the wicked often walk in evil like their fathers, and sometimes exceed them in evil. But we do not deny that some children took a lesson from their parents, and insisted on living with God.

4.3.0.en: And though they put forth branches for a time, because they are not firmly rooted the wind shakes them, and the force of the whirlwind plucks them up. [4]

4.3.1.en: The wicked rejoice when they see their children as though they were firm branches in the tree, but as long as the root itself is not firm, what can we expect for the branches except that the whirlwinds will kill them? Therefore he says: "for a time."

4.3.2.en: The wise man likens the wicked to roots without depth in the earth, which find no spiritual nourishment to refresh them; therefore the children or branches mostly imbibe evil from their parents, and become like branches the winds shake, and the storms pluck up before the time of fruit. If they bear fruit, it does not bring fruit good to eat.

4.3.3.en: Thus the wise man warns the wicked not only against relying on abundance of wealth and power but even on abundance of children, for all these are without profit as long as they are not in fellowship with God.

4.3.4.en: "A foolish son is a grief to his father, and bitterness to her that bare him" (Prov 17:25).

4.3.5.en: "A foolish son is the calamity of his father" (Prov 19:13).

4.3.6.en: "For I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me" (Ex 20:5).

4.3.7.en: "Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation" (Ex 34:7).

4.3.8.en: "The LORD is longsuffering, and of great mercy, forgiving iniquity and transgression, and by no means clearing the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation" (Num 14:18).

4.3.9.en: "Thou shalt not bow down thyself unto them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me" (Deut 5:9).

4.3.10.en: The Lord's words here do not mean that God takes vengeance for Himself upon the children for what their fathers did. But He wishes to affirm His longsuffering, for He leaves the wicked for repentance year after year, and generation after generation, and when man is determined to do evil he is disciplined in the third or fourth generation, not for the sins of their fathers, but because of the children's insistence on evil conduct after the manner of their fathers.

4.4.0.en: So its young branches are broken off before they grow, and its fruit is unprofitable, not ripe to eat, and good for nothing. [5]

4.4.1.en: The wicked look forward to the growth of their children, for this is their hope, but often these children go bad and become a burden to their parents, who do not see in them the desired fruit, that is, the immortalizing of their memory; even if they succeed in practicing some of their works, this fruit is unprofitable and is not fit to eat or for anything else. This is the fruit of evil in the lives of the wicked, as in the lives of their children, if they walk in the evil way of their fathers.

4.4.2.en: * It behooves us to remember that in the world to come no one is purified from his least faults unless he is qualified for that by purification through his good works (springing from faith) which he practiced in this life.

4.5.0.en: For children born of the sinful sleep are witnesses at the inquiry to the wickedness of their parents. [6]

4.5.1.en: The righteous, even in their relations with their wives, are governed by the law of chastity and purity, so that the bodily relationship is an expression of pure, clean love and the mutual respect between them. But the wicked, even in their relations with their lawful wives, are governed by the law of violent lust, and what occupies each of the spouses is the satisfaction of purely bodily desires; therefore the children, who are the fruit of these lusts, are often affected by the evil of their fathers.

4.6.s.en: 2. Man's honor is in his holiness, not in his age

4.6.0.en: 7 But the righteous, though death overtake him quickly, shall rest in repose. 8 For honorable old age is not that which is of long duration, nor is it measured by the number of years. 9 But the gray hair of man is understanding, and the age of old age is the life free from blemish. 10 He was pleasing to God and so He loved him, and he lived among sinners and so He translated him. 11 He snatched him away lest evil should change his mind, or deceit lead his soul astray. 12 For the witchery of vanities obscures the good, and the whirl of desire unsettles the sound mind. 13 He was brought to perfection in a few days; so he fulfilled many years. 14 And since his soul was pleasing to the Lord, he was quickly taken out from among evils. But the peoples saw and did not understand and did not lay this up in their hearts: 15 that His grace and mercy are for His chosen, and His visitation for His saints. 16 But the righteous who has died judges the hypocrites who remain after him, and the youth quickly perfected judges the old age of the wicked with its many years. 17 For they see the death of the wise man, and do not understand what the Lord intended for him, and why He translated him to His safekeeping. 18 They see and despise, and the Lord laughs them to scorn. 19 They shall fall hereafter with a shameful fall, and shall be a disgrace among the dead for ever. For He shall dash them, speechless, with downcast eyes, and pluck them up from the foundations, and bring them to utter ruin; and they shall be in torment, and their memory shall perish. 20 They shall come fearful at the remembrance of their sins, and their iniquities shall accuse them to their face.

4.6.1.en: It is observed that some of the righteous die at an early age. Here God gives us assurance that they leave the world of toil, or the valley of tears, to cross over to eternal rest where they settle in the bosom of the Father.

4.6.2.en: Thus honorable old age is not in the multitude of years, but in the practice of righteousness and the enjoyment of life with God. Some young people in age have the wisdom of the elders and their dignity which they have acquired from God, just as some elders, in spite of the length of their lives, walk in folly.

4.6.3.en: Whoever loves God enjoys divine wisdom and receives true happiness, even in his death he receives a better happiness, which cannot be expressed.

4.6.4.en: Whoever trusts in God, He grants him to achieve a complete life surpassing his age, and he is made worthy of heavenly glories; in other words he achieves in a few years more than another achieves in long years, and it is said of them truly "redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16).

4.6.5.en: But as for the righteous, though death overtake him quickly, he shall rest in repose. [7]

4.6.6.en: God had previously promised the righteous a good old age, and threatened the wicked with an early evil death. And it was fitting for believers to grasp this promise and that warning spiritually. For the righteous, even if he lives one day, is reckoned by the Lord as a thousand years, and the wicked, even if he lives a thousand years, is in the eye of the Lord as one fruitless day.

4.6.7.en: Here for the first time in the Old Testament he deals with the problem of the death of young righteous people, because he departs from the valley of tears to rest with God. For even if he dies young he is reckoned as a venerable wise old man honored with holy virtues.

4.6.8.en: St. Jerome wrote a letter to his old friend Heliodorus, Bishop of Alrirum, on his losing his sister's son, the young priest Nepotian, in which he said:

4.6.9.en: * O good Jesus! How he used to groan and sigh! How he hurried and fled from the eyes of all! For, for the first and only time he became angry with his uncle, complaining of the weight of the responsibility cast upon him, very heavy, and that his young age was not suited to the priesthood. But the more he resisted this the more he clung to the hearts of all. His refusal of the priesthood only made him worthy of the work whose responsibility he refused to bear. He became the more worthy as he declared his feeling of unworthiness. We also in our days saw in him our Timothy (that is, like the young Timothy, the disciple of the Apostle Paul, who was ordained bishop), and we also saw in him good wisdom like the gray-haired people.

4.6.10.en: St. Jerome The author has given light on this through the story of Enoch, who pleased the Lord and so He translated him (Gen 5:21-24).

4.6.11.en: Believers did not fear death even if it came hastily, or took place in any form. Death did not shake the faith of Christians, for the apologist Tatian says:

4.6.12.en: [Even if the fires destroy my body...

4.6.13.en: And even if it be scattered among the rivers and seas, and wild beasts tear it into pieces, I shall be gathered into the rich storehouses of God...

4.6.14.en: And when God the King wills, He will restore my visible being, for Himself alone, to its original state.]

4.6.15.en: * The death of the righteous has become a falling asleep, indeed it has become life.

4.6.16.en: St. Basil the Great * Many of our people die this (bodily) death, and so are freed from this world. This death, which (the people of the world) count a calamity, the servants of God see as a departure to salvation.

4.6.17.en: The righteous die like the wicked without distinction.... but the righteous are called to rest, and the wicked to punishment.

4.6.18.en: Great peace is given to believers, and punishment to unbelievers.

4.6.19.en: * As for rest, what do we find in the world but constant war with Satan, and struggle in perpetual battle against his arrows and swords?! Our war is against the love of money and pride and anger and love of display, and our struggle is constant against bodily lusts and the allurements of the world.

4.6.20.en: For man's mind is besieged by the enemy from every side, and the assaults of Satan surround it from every direction. And with effort the mind is able to defend, and it can scarcely resist in every spot. For if it despised the love of money, the passions rose in it. And if it conquered the passions, the love of display sprang up. And if it triumphed over the love of display, anger and pride were kindled in it, and drunkenness with wine allured it, and envy tore its harmony with others, and jealousy corrupted its friendships.

4.6.21.en: Thus the spirit suffers every day many persecutions like these, and great dangers like these oppress the heart, and yet the heart still rejoices in its remaining long here among the wars of Satan! Though it would have been more fitting for our longings and desires to be set on hastening to go to Christ, by way of hastened death. For the Lord Himself taught us, saying: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, That ye shall weep and lament, but the world shall rejoice: and ye shall be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy" (Jn 16:20).

4.6.22.en: Who of us does not wish to be without sorrow?!

4.6.23.en: Who of us does not long to hasten to obtain joy?!

4.6.24.en: The Lord Himself also declared the time of the turning of our sorrow into joy by saying: "But I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you" (Jn 16:20). As long as our joy lies in seeing Christ... what blindness strikes our mind, and what foolishness befalls us if we love the sorrows of the world and its afflictions and tears more than hastening toward the joy that is not taken from us?!

4.7.0.en: The Martyr St. Cyprian For honorable old age does not consist in length of time, nor is it measured by the number of years. [8]

4.7.1.en: The wicked gloat over the righteous who die at a young age, supposing that they did not enjoy the pleasures of life, and at the same time did not receive the honor of the elders.

4.7.2.en: They suppose that the elder's honor lies in his white hair and the length of his years and his experiences, but honor is not measured by a man's age, nor by his mere experiences; for his experiences may be evil and he holds fast to them, counting them wisdom itself.

4.7.3.en: * The elder is he who is first to go ahead and hear about the work.

4.7.4.en: The elder is he who lives a great age in faith.

4.7.5.en: The elder is he whose age is esteemed, and whose long time is without wrinkle.

4.8.0.en: St. Ambrose But wisdom is the youth of man, and the age of old age is the life free from blemish. [9]

4.8.1.en: The Holy Bible points to the youth of man as a sign of strength and vitality, saying: "thy youth is renewed like the eagle's" (Ps 103:5). So the believer does not grow old spiritually, that is, weakness and incapacity do not overtake him. And it also points at times to old age as a sign of wisdom and balance in conduct; so the believer carries the spirit of youth in work, and the spirit of elders in making his decisions.

4.8.2.en: Here the wise man declares that in order to carry this spirit we look to wisdom as the guide of our work, so that we work with strength, but not with rashness, and we look to the life free from blemish as a support for us in making our wise decisions; for there is no separation between wisdom and righteousness.

4.8.3.en: St. Palladius presents to us a wonderful picture of spiritual leaders not relying on their old age, saying of the great elder Macarius of Alexandria: [I took an opportunity one day and sat at the door of the elder, who was then very advanced in his days, having reached a hundred years. And I imagined that he was older than all men and more holy, and he had lost all his teeth. He was alone, yet I kept listening, and I heard him speaking and moving, for he was wrestling with himself and with Satan. He was saying to himself: ‘What do you want, wicked old man? You have oil and wine, and what more do you want, greedy gray-haired old man?’ Thus he rebuked himself. Then he would say to Satan also: ‘Am I still in your debt for anything? You will find nothing of yours in me! Get away from me.’ And as though muttering, he kept on saying to himself: ‘Come, you gray-haired, lustful old man, you treacherous horse, how long shall I remain with you?’]

4.8.4.en: * Just as not all young people are alike in their zeal in spirit or equal in learning sound doctrines and manners, so also not all elders are alike in perfection and virtue.

4.8.5.en: For true (spiritual) wealth is not measured by gray hair, but by striving from youth and according to the crowns of their former works...

4.8.6.en: For honorable old age is not that which is of long duration, nor is it measured by the number of years. "But the gray hair of man is understanding, and the age of old age is the life free from blemish" (Wis 4:9)...

4.8.7.en: Therefore we should not imitate any elder whose head is covered with gray hair... but follow in the footsteps of those who from their youth were distinguished by a fitting life worthy of all praise, who were trained according to the traditions of the Fathers, and not according to themselves.

4.8.8.en: Some passed into old age through lukewarmness and laziness; these God rebukes through the prophet, saying: "Strangers have devoured his wealth, and he knoweth not, and it is sprinkled upon the gray hairs, and he knoweth not" (Hos 7:9)... Satan uses the gray hairs of these to deceive the young, through their false appearance of dignity, deceiving those who needed to strive in the way of perfection through their counsels... causing them (the young) to fall into indifference or deadly despair, through the teachings of such elders and their works.

4.9.0.en: Father Moses He became pleasing to God, so he was beloved, and since he was living among sinners, he was translated [10]

4.9.1.en: Here he speaks of Enoch, who was righteous, so the Lord loved him and translated him from among sinners. And the Scripture says: "the righteous is gathered from before evil" (Isa 57:1).

4.9.3.en: "No one like Enoch was created on the earth, who was translated from the earth" (Sir 49:16).

4.9.4.en: "Enoch pleased the Lord and was translated, and he will call the generations to repentance" (Sir 44:16).

4.9.5.en: * Good are the wings of love, the true wings that flutter on the lips of the Apostles; the wings of fire that utter pure speech (Acts 2:2-3). On those wings Enoch flew when he was caught up to heaven (Gen 5:24).

4.9.6.en: * Enoch sought God in hope, and therefore it is thought that he was translated; thus man appears "man" only when he puts his hope in God. Also the clear and true understanding of the text (Gen 5:18-24) is that whoever puts his hope in God does not dwell on earth, but is translated, and then cleaves to God.

4.9.7.en: St. Ambrose * This event (the translation of Enoch) shows that one righteous man is more precious to God than many sinners.

4.10.0.en: St. Augustine Yes, he was snatched away lest evil corrupt his understanding, or deceit seduce his soul. [11]

4.10.1.en: God often allows a person to die at an early age, because God loves him and sees that he has matured spiritually and qualified for the crown. And also since He sees evil increasing around him, He snatches him so that evil may not corrupt his thoughts and concepts. And since deceitful cheats besiege him, He does not leave him lest deceit creep into him. What occupies God's heart is not the length of man's life on earth, but his readiness for eternal glory.

4.10.2.en: Some Fathers see that with the killing of Abel Adam's psychology was shattered, therefore God wished to comfort him, and allowed him to see the righteous Enoch translated from earth to heaven as a man beloved by God and very dear to Him.

4.10.3.en: * Some say that while Adam was looking (at Enoch), God translated him to Paradise, lest Adam think that Enoch had been killed like Abel and grieve for him. This also happened so that Adam might be comforted by this righteous son of his, and realize that all who imitate him, whether before death or after the resurrection, will have their meeting in Paradise.

4.10.4.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * This statement concerns those who, after being baptized and growing in the godly life, were not permitted to remain long on earth, since they became perfect not through length of years, but through the grace of heavenly wisdom.

4.10.5.en: St. Augustine * It was pleasing in the eyes of God that Enoch was made worthy to depart from the poison of this world. But the Holy Spirit also teaches us through Solomon that those who please God are taken from here at an early age, and are quickly freed, lest through their remaining a long time in this world they be corrupted by dealings with the world.

4.10.6.en: The Martyr St. Cyprian * If no one grieves for Enoch who was translated (Gen 5:24) when the world was at peace and wars had not been kindled, but rather congratulates him, as the Scripture says of him: "He was snatched away lest evil corrupt his understanding" (Wis 4:11), how much more can this be said with greater justification where the dangers of the world have multiplied for an unsettled life?

4.10.7.en: He was snatched away lest he fall into the hands of the barbarians, he was taken lest he see the destruction of the whole earth, and the end of the world, and the burial of his relatives, and the death of his fellow citizens, and above all this and more bitter than any death, lest he see the holy virgins and widows corrupted.

4.11.0.en: St. Ambrose For the witchery of vanity obscures what is good, and the wandering of desire corrupts the simple mind. [12]

4.11.1.en: The Apostle Paul gives us a warning that we may have a spirit of discernment so that we do not enter into mixing with the wicked, nor dwell with them under one roof, but love them and serve them and seek their salvation by prayer and fasting, without falling into condemning them.

4.11.2.en: God knows the seriousness of evil and corruption, and how some persons are exposed to walking in evil through their contact with the wicked. And as the Apostle says: "Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners" (1 Cor 15:33). For evil, like witchcraft, tries to corrupt the good and to dominate simple minds.

4.11.3.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic presented to us in his book "Against the Heathen" an exposition of the practical testimony, through the life of the gods, about the corruption, lusts and baseness that marked it, and he mentioned many examples of this.

4.11.4.en: * We see people who were quiet and dignified when they entered into friendship with a rowdy and disreputable people, their good morals corrupted through evil discussions. They turn into people of the same kind as those who go down in every way. This sometimes happens with mature people, who have proved that they lived in their youth in greater purity than their life in advanced age, when the opportunity came to them for a loose life.

4.11.5.en: * Make every effort to withdraw from the wicked person, for as soon as he departs from you Christ dwells in you.

4.12.0.en: Origen Having reached perfection in a short time, he fulfilled a long time. [13]

4.12.1.en: Although God longs to preserve the lives of His righteous children so that evil may not creep into them, these righteous were able to reach perfection in a short time, and their lives achieved their mission, and became in the eyes of God as though they were a long life; for one day with the Lord is as a thousand years (Ps 90:4).

4.12.2.en: St. Jerome wrote to Salvina, comforting her on the death of her husband Nebridius, who was one of the men of the royal palace, and was young in age, but what he did made him, despite his youth, a venerable elder. In it he said: [He fell asleep in the Lord, he slept with his fathers, full of days and of light like one in a good old age. For "wisdom is the gray hair unto men" (cf. Wis 4:9). In a short time he fulfilled a long time (cf. Wis 4:13).

4.12.3.en: And his soul was pleasing to the Lord, and therefore He quickly took him out from among evils.

4.13.0.en: And the people saw and did not understand, nor did it come into their mind. [14]

4.13.1.en: Since his life was the object of God's pleasure and satisfaction, the Lord hastened to bring him out from the midst of evils, even if his people did not grasp the mystery of his swift translation.

4.13.2.en: Finally, the death of the righteous at an early age is a grace and mercy from God, and a divine visitation of them.

4.13.3.en: St. Jerome wrote to the lady Theodora, comforting her on the death of her righteous husband Lucinius, in which he said:

4.13.4.en: * As is recorded in the Book of Wisdom, he was taken lest evil change his understanding, for his soul was pleasing to the Lord, and in a short time he fulfilled a long time (cf. Wis 4:11-14). Rightly it behooves us to weep for our own state, that every day we wrestle with our sins, being stained with vices, and wounds come upon us while we render an account for every idle word (Mt 12:39). Now he is victorious and freed from every anxiety, looking down upon us from on high, helping us in our striving; nay, and he prepares for you a place beside him, for his love for you and his tenderness toward you remain as they were. He does not look upon you as a husband, but as he decided to deal with you even while on earth, as a sister to him.

4.13.5.en: * Perhaps he was taken (translated) lest evil change his understanding... for his soul had pleased the Lord, therefore He hastened to take him from among men (cf. Wis 4:14), lest in the journey of a long life he enter into untrodden mazes.

4.13.6.en: In truth we ought to mourn for the dead, but only for those whom Gehenna snatches and hell devours.

4.13.7.en: But we, since in our departure we are in the company of guardian angels, and meet Jesus Christ, ought rather to grieve that we remain long in the tent of death (2 Cor 5:4). For whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord" (2 Cor 5:6). Our only longing is that which the psalmist expressed: "Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged for me...".

4.14.0.en: St. Jerome That His grace and mercy are for His saints, and His visitation for His chosen. [15]

4.14.1.en: The children of God are distinguished by true wisdom, so they perceive God's purposes, and His plan for them is unveiled to them, but the wicked who cling to their sins and rely upon their own minds and emotions alone are unable to perceive God's purposes.

4.14.2.en: The wicked go on in their evil and err in their evaluation of life's events. They see in the righteous life and worship and service a deprivation of the enjoyment of the world's lusts as they enjoy them, so they accuse the righteous of folly and stupidity, because they do not share with them their pleasures. While they go on in their evils, behold the Lord from the heavens laughs at their ignorance.

4.14.3.en: * The people outside the Church may suppose that we are sorrowful, but in reality we are always rejoicing. We seem as though poor, and in truth we have innumerable riches, spiritual and material. As usual the Christian life is the exact opposite of what appears on the surface.

4.14.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * The spirit of the holy man is refreshed by thinking on godly matters and practicing them, for the spirit strives for what is good (and finds its delight in it).

4.14.5.en: St. Didymus the Blind But when death comes the situation changes completely; there is no longer an opportunity for correction, so despair comes upon the wicked, and they are filled with misery and bitterness, and bow their heads in shame, because death has uprooted them from their lusts and their evil thoughts which did not profit them. Their memory on earth itself becomes a disgrace and shame.

4.14.6.en: The moments of death are most terrifying for the wicked, for the moment comes of the revealing of the truth and the lifting of the veil from all deceit.

4.14.7.en: After death the wicked, in terror, go from fear to fear; their mouths are stopped so that their very iniquities speak, bearing witness against them.

4.15.0.en: But the righteous who has died condemns the wicked who remain alive, and the gray hair that was quickly ended judges the old age of the wicked with its many years. [16]

4.15.1.en: He highlights the blessings of early death for the righteous, speaking of the efficacy of this matter and its effect on the wicked, for in the early death of the righteous there is a rebuke to them, for despite the swiftness of their departure, they accomplished works which the wicked elders did not accomplish. Their life on earth ended quickly, but it remains a witness against the wicked old age which did not bear proper fruit.

4.16.0.en: For they see the end of the wise man, and do not understand what the Lord willed concerning him, and why He put him in safety. [17]

4.16.1.en: The wicked elders look upon the righteous in bitterness, and compare themselves with them, these who died in the youth of their age. For they, being old, fear death and dread it, while the righteous were in safety and peace even in giving up their spirits.

4.16.2.en: The wicked stand in amazement, and as the psalmist says: "Let the lying lips be put to silence; which speak grievous things proudly and contemptuously against the righteous" (Ps 31:18). "For the arms of the wicked shall be broken: but the LORD upholdeth the righteous" (Ps 37:17). And the wise man says: "The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked cometh in his stead" (Prov 11:8), "A man shall not be established by wickedness: but the root of the righteous shall not be moved" (Prov 12:3). "There shall no evil happen to the just: but the wicked shall be filled with mischief" (Prov 12:21).

4.16.3.en: * If anyone proves that his work abides (1 Cor 3:14), he shall receive his reward. He will be like the three youths in the furnace of fire (Dan 3:1-10), he receives as his reward heavenly life with glory.

4.16.4.en: * Those who are called in peace must aim at longsuffering so that the laws of peace may not be broken.

4.16.5.en: Father Ambrosiaster * The man whose armor is of gold crosses through a river of fire, and comes out shining with greater splendor, but he who crosses it with straw will lose it and himself perish with it.

4.16.6.en: * As our love for the coming of God intensifies there is no kind of sin that is not destroyed!

4.17.0.en: St. John Chrysostom They see and despise, but the Lord laughs them to scorn. [18]

4.17.1.en: The wicked enter into a struggle between their contact with the security of the righteous and their inner peace, and their claim that they pretend to peace, having lost everything! They make light of the lives of the righteous, so the Lord mocks them. And as the psalmist says: "He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision" (Ps 2:4).

4.17.2.en: And after that they become a despised corpse, and a disgrace among the dead for ever and ever.

4.18.0.en: For He shall dash them, silent and with bowed heads, and shake them from their foundations, and they shall be left desolate to the end, and they shall be in torment and their memory shall perish. [19]

4.18.1.en: However long their life, they will one day become a despised corpse, dying without hope of enjoying eternal glories. They enter the tombs in disgrace and shame, in silence they bow their heads downward, for they have no excuse for the evil they committed. Death shakes their foundations, since they placed all their hope in temporal things, and they become like a barren desert without fruit. They enter into the torment that awaits them, and their memory vanishes completely.

4.18.2.en: Here he adds the destiny of the wicked after death and before the coming of the Day of Judgment, which the book of the prophet Isaiah often portrayed:

4.18.3.en: "But thou art cast out of thy grave like an abominable branch, and as the raiment of those that are slain, thrust through with a sword, that go down to the stones of the pit; as a carcase trodden under feet" (Isa 14:19).

4.18.4.en: "And they shall go forth, and look upon the carcases of the men that have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they shall be an abhorring unto all flesh" (Isa 66:24).

4.19.0.en: And when their sins are reckoned they shall come fearful, and their iniquities shall accuse them to their face. [20]

4.19.1.en: They await the Day of Judgment in great terror, because the one who judges them is their iniquities. Although the Lord is the Judge, He is merciful and seeks the salvation of all! But they gave God the back and gave iniquities the face, and so fell into the fruit of the iniquities which they chose by their free will.

4.19.2.en: Here the Book of Wisdom presents to us a wonderful concept of God's wrath and His judgment upon the wicked, for He did not wish the destruction of anyone, but He sanctifies freedom of will, so whoever throws himself into destruction by his will reaps what he desired.

4.19.3.en: * "Enter into the Kingdom, for I was hungry and you fed me"; therefore you will enter into the Kingdom not because you have not sinned, but because by your almsgiving you have removed your sins. Likewise to the others: "Go into the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels." They also are sinners, since they are rooted in their sins and slow in their fear of them. When they set their sins before their minds, can they from any side dare to say that they are condemned without right, and that this statement issuing from such a righteous judge has been pronounced against them without desert? Looking to their consciences and all the wounds of their spirits, how do they dare to say that we are condemned unjustly? It has been said of them in the Book of Wisdom: "their iniquities shall accuse them to their face" (Wis 4:20); they will see without doubt that they are justly condemned for their sins and evils. And yet in its place He says to them that it is not because of what you think but "for I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat"; for if you had turned away from all these works of yours and turned to me you would have been saved from all your crimes and sins by your almsgiving, your almsgiving would now have saved you and acquitted you of the great sins, for "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy" (Mt 5:7), but now "Go into the everlasting fire, for judgment without mercy shall be to him that hath shewed no mercy" (Jas 2:13).

4.19.5.en: Let me possess You, O immortal righteousness!

4.19.6.en: * You created me in Your image, so my soul longs for immortality.

4.19.7.en: But my hand stretched out to record a covenant with death!
